subject: english-literature
title: Context and Comparison
welcome_lead: Even with an unseen poem, you bring context. And many exam tasks ask comparison. Master both moves.
meta_desc: Contextualising unseen poetry and comparative tasks at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You can now situate the unseen poem in tradition and pair it with another for confident comparison.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A poem about trenches, gas and barbed wire situates itself in the First World War without naming dates.

Always justify contextual claims with textual evidence.
For comparison, decide the axis. Same theme, different mode? Same form, different politics? Begin with the axis and let details follow.
Owen's Dulce et Decorum Est and Brooke's The Soldier share the war theme but oppose it tonally. The contrast becomes the essay.

mcqs.q: Why does historical context matter when reading literature?
options: Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
Texts emerge from and respond to specific historical conditions — context illuminates references, assumptions and arguments that might otherwise be invisible.
Context just means writing about what the author had for breakfast.
Context is required because all texts are about history.

mcqs.q: What did Romantic poets value in nature?
options: Romantic poets just liked to write about pretty landscapes.
Context is required because all texts are about history.
Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
Nature as a source of spiritual insight and emotional truth, accessed through imagination — not picturesque scenery for its own sake.
It means authors can never make mistakes when writing.
Context is required because all texts are about history.
It means it is wrong to write fiction.
The claim that judging a text by what the author 'intended' is fallacious — the text's meaning lies in the work itself, not the author's stated or guessed intentions.
